questions.stem: A 46 year old man is 6 days after an open left inguinal hernia repair. His wound has become sore and red over 2 days. There is 3 cm of warm, tender erythema around the incision but no discharge and no fluctuance. He feels well. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cellulitis around a wound with no pus, no collection and no systemic upset is a superficial SSI. A seroma or haematoma is a swelling, not spreading erythema.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: 6 days after an open left inguinal hernia repair
steps.x: Red, warm, tender skin around the incision in a well patient: infection confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Superficial surgical site infection.

elim: Nothing points below the skin: no pus from the fascia, no wound breakdown, no systemic upset.
Would give pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus and a toxic patient.
A collection of clear fluid that is fluctuant, not a warm, red, tender wound.
A tense bruised swelling early after surgery, not spreading erythema at day 6.

steps.x: **D. Superficial surgical site infection.** Erythema and tenderness confined to the skin around the incision = superficial SSI.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman is 5 days after an emergency caesarean section. Her BMI is 38. Her Pfannenstiel wound is red, hot and discharging thick yellow pus. A wound swab Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters, and the organism is coagulase positive. Her temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: S. aureus is the most common cause of SSI because it lives on the skin; Gram-positive coagulase-positive clusters confirm it. Streptococci grow in chains.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive identify S. aureus, the commonest SSI organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Staphylococcus aureus.

elim: A Gram-negative anaerobe of the bowel; it does not form Gram-positive clusters.
A Gram-negative rod, seen more in bowel-related organ/space infection.
A Gram-negative rod, typically in burns or long-standing wounds.
Gram-positive cocci in chains, and coagulase negative.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** Most SSIs are skin flora: Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is 9 days after a midline laparotomy for small bowel obstruction. Pus is discharging from the lower wound. On exploring the wound at the bedside, the infection extends through the subcutaneous fat to the rectus sheath, which is soft and grey. A CT scan shows no intra-abdominal collection. Her temperature is 38.1°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Infection involving fascia or muscle is a deep SSI. Superficial SSI is confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue; organ/space SSI involves the cavity, which CT shows is clear.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: extends through the subcutaneous fat to the rectus sheath
steps.x: Infection reaching the fascia, without an intra-abdominal collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Deep surgical site infection.

elim: CT shows no intra-abdominal collection or free fluid, and the problem is in the wound layers.
That involves the peritoneal cavity itself, but CT shows no collection.
A tiny superficial abscess at one suture, not infection down to the fascia.
That stops at skin and subcutaneous tissue; here the fascia is involved.

steps.x: **B. Deep surgical site infection.** Classify by depth: skin/fat = superficial, fascia/muscle = deep, operated cavity = organ/space.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man is 3 weeks after a left total hip replacement. He has increasing pain in the hip on walking and at night. The scar is healed, but the hip is warm and movement is painful. His temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. Investigations: CRP 118 mg/L (<5) and WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (4–11).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Septic arthritis of the native knee
questions.e: Joint infection after orthopaedic surgery is an organ/space SSI: the infection is in the space entered at operation. A superficial SSI would show a red, discharging scar.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: 3 weeks after a left total hip replacement
the hip is warm and movement is painful
steps.x: Fever and raised markers with a healed scar point to infection in the operated joint space.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Organ/space surgical site infection.

elim: Gives calf or thigh swelling, not a hot painful joint with a CRP of 118.
Sudden pain with a shortened, rotated leg, not fever and raised markers.
The knee was not operated on; the symptoms are in the replaced hip.
The scar is healed; the infection is in the joint itself.

steps.x: **C. Organ/space surgical site infection.** Infection in the joint or cavity that was operated on = organ/space SSI.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is 7 days after a laparoscopic appendicectomy for a perforated appendix. His port sites are clean and dry. He has a swinging fever, lower abdominal pain, diarrhoea and a tender mass on rectal examination. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. The site of pain is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Lower abdominal pain with a tender pelvic mass.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An abscess in the space entered at surgery is an organ/space SSI, the most dangerous type. Clean port sites rule out superficial infection.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: port sites are clean and dry
steps.x: Clean wounds, swinging fever and a pelvic mass after contaminated surgery: a collection in the operated space.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pelvic abscess (organ/space surgical site infection).

elim: Gives diarrhoea after antibiotics but not a tender pelvic mass with clean wounds and a swinging fever.
A bulge at a port site, not fever and a pelvic mass.
The port sites are clean and dry.
Gives dysuria and frequency, not a tender mass on rectal examination.

steps.x: **B. Pelvic abscess (organ/space surgical site infection).** Swinging fever + clean wound after bowel surgery = think collection (organ/space SSI).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is seen in pre-assessment before an elective open inguinal hernia repair. He has type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c of 82 mmol/mol, a BMI of 36 and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. He takes metformin and amlodipine. He had his appendix removed aged 12. He is blood group O.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of surgical site infection?
questions.e: Diabetes, obesity, smoking, immunosuppression and emergency or contaminated surgery raise SSI risk. Elective surgery, blood group and amlodipine do not.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Diabetes (badly controlled), obesity and smoking are all on the risk list; of these options only diabetes is offered.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Poorly controlled diabetes.

elim: Not a recognised risk factor for wound infection.
Blood group has no effect on SSI risk.
Elective surgery carries a lower risk than emergency surgery.
Previous surgery elsewhere does not raise the risk of this wound becoming infected.

steps.x: **D. Poorly controlled diabetes.** SSI risk factors: diabetes, obesity, smoking, immunosuppression, poor wound care, emergency/contaminated surgery.

questions.stem: A surgical audit compares wound infection rates after five operations performed in the same hospital. All patients are non-smokers without diabetes, and all received standard skin preparation. One operation had a wound infection rate four times higher than the others.
questions.q: Which operation is most likely to have had the highest surgical site infection rate?
questions.e: Emergency and contaminated surgery are risk factors; faecal peritonitis is a dirty, emergency field. The other operations are elective and clean or clean-contaminated.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Emergency, contaminated (dirty) surgery carries the highest SSI risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emergency laparotomy for faecal peritonitis.

elim: Clean-contaminated and elective, with small port wounds.
A clean, elective operation with the lowest risk.
A clean operation that does not enter a contaminated viscus.
A clean operation done under strict asepsis.

steps.x: **E. Emergency laparotomy for faecal peritonitis.** Emergency + contaminated field = highest SSI risk.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman is 8 days after a right mastectomy. Her wound has been red and painful for 4 days despite oral antibiotics. Over the lateral end of the scar there is a 3 cm tender, warm swelling. Her temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the swelling?
questions.e: An abscess in an infected wound is felt as fluctuance; antibiotics alone fail because pus needs draining. Crepitus would suggest necrotising infection.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: red and painful for 4 days despite oral antibiotics
steps.x: A tender warm swelling in an infected wound that is not settling on antibiotics is a pus collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluctuance.

elim: Suggests gas in tissue from necrotising infection, which would make her very unwell.
Seen in simple cellulitis without a collection; it does not explain a tender swelling despite antibiotics.
Suggests a false aneurysm, not an infected wound.
Seen with a clear fluid cyst, not pus.

steps.x: **B. Fluctuance.** Infected wound not settling + tender swelling = abscess: feel for fluctuance.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman is 2 days after a caesarean section. She has severe pain spreading from her wound across her lower abdomen, much worse than she would expect. The skin has dusky purple patches and crackles under the fingers. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 132 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading dusky skin, crepitus and shock define necrotising soft tissue infection, a surgical emergency. A deep SSI does not cause gas or necrosis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: much worse than she would expect
steps.x: Pain out of proportion, skin necrosis, crepitus and systemic toxicity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Necrotising soft tissue infection.

elim: Gives a tender bruised swelling, not fever, shock and crepitus.
Causes pus in the fascia but not rapid spread, skin necrosis and gas in the tissue.
Can cause tachycardia and hypotension, but not skin changes over the wound.
Causes local erythema in a well patient, not septic shock and crepitus.

steps.x: **C. Necrotising soft tissue infection.** Pain out of proportion + crepitus + toxic patient = necrotising soft tissue infection.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with type 2 diabetes is 3 days after an open repair of a perforated duodenal ulcer. He is in severe pain at the wound and needs repeated morphine. The erythema around the wound has spread 8 cm in 4 hours. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination of the wound?
o: Clear serous fluid in a fluctuant swelling
questions.e: Necrotising soft tissue infection produces gas in the tissues, felt as crepitus, alongside skin necrosis. An abscess develops more slowly and causes localised fluctuance.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Rapid spread, pain needing repeated opioids and shock suggest necrotising infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Crepitus in the surrounding skin.

elim: Spreading erythema and severe pain would not occur with a clean wound.
Describes a seroma, not a rapidly spreading toxic infection.
Describes an abscess, which develops slowly and does not spread 8 cm in hours.
Suggests a false aneurysm, not a spreading infection.

steps.x: **C. Crepitus in the surrounding skin.** Necrotising infection: look for crepitus (gas in tissue) and skin necrosis.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman is 5 days after an open right hemicolectomy. Her midline wound has become more painful, with spreading erythema and a purulent discharge. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Investigations: lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2).
questions.q: Which feature most strongly indicates that this infection has become life-threatening?
questions.e: Hypotension shows organ hypoperfusion: this is sepsis secondary to SSI and needs emergency management. Fever, pus and erythema occur in uncomplicated wound infection too.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Tachycardia, hypotension and a raised lactate: sepsis from the wound.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood pressure of 88/52 mmHg.

elim: Close to normal and does not by itself show organ dysfunction.
Indicates infection, and is present in superficial SSI in well patients.
Shows local spread but does not by itself show sepsis.
Fever occurs in many simple wound infections.

steps.x: **A. Blood pressure of 88/52 mmHg.** In SSI, hypotension and tachycardia = sepsis: escalate now.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with a BMI of 41 is 10 days after an emergency caesarean section. Her wound has been discharging pus for 5 days. Today the skin edges have separated along 6 cm, exposing yellow fat with slough in the base. The rectus sheath is intact. Her temperature is 37.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication to have occurred?
questions.e: Wound breakdown is a complication of SSI; the intact sheath makes this superficial dehiscence rather than a burst abdomen. It will need debridement and later closure (re-suturing) once clean.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: skin edges have separated along 6 cm
steps.x: An infected wound has broken open, but only down to fat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Superficial wound dehiscence.

elim: That is full-thickness dehiscence; here the rectus sheath is intact.
A late bulge through a healed scar, not separated skin edges at day 10.
She would be toxic with crepitus and rapidly spreading skin necrosis.
A fluid collection under intact skin, not separated edges.

steps.x: **D. Superficial wound dehiscence.** SSI can cause wound dehiscence; check whether the fascia is intact.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is 6 days after a below-knee amputation for peripheral arterial disease. He reports throbbing stump pain, malaise and a foul smell from the dressing. The wound edges are swollen and red, and one area is slow to heal with a small amount of pus. His temperature is 37.9°C. CRP is 96 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain, a red swollen wound with pus, foul smell, delayed healing, malaise and raised inflammatory markers are the usual presentation of SSI.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: slow to heal with a small amount of pus
steps.x: Wound pain, swelling, pus, foul smell, delayed healing, fever and raised CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Surgical site infection.

elim: Causes leg swelling but not a foul-smelling, discharging wound.
Causes sharp shooting pain months later, not fever and pus.
Pain felt in the missing limb, with a normal wound.
A bruised swelling early on, not pus and a foul smell.

steps.x: **E. Surgical site infection.** Painful red wound + pus + foul smell + raised CRP = SSI.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman is 4 weeks after a right total knee replacement. The knee is hot, swollen and painful to move. The wound has healed. Her temperature is 38.1°C. Her CRP is 140 mg/L. The orthopaedic team suspect a deep (organ/space) infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Clinical assessment with culture and imaging of the joint
questions.e: The gold standard for SSI is clinical diagnosis, plus wound culture and imaging if deep infection is suspected. A skin swab cannot sample a deep joint infection.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: 4 weeks after a right total knee replacement
steps.x: Deep infection is suspected, so the diagnosis rests on clinical findings plus culture and imaging.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical assessment with culture and imaging of the joint.

elim: Enough for superficial SSI, but deep infection needs culture and imaging.
Cannot show infection early and gives no organism.
Delays diagnosis; a trend does not identify the site or organism.
The wound has healed; a skin swab does not sample a deep infection.

steps.x: **B. Clinical assessment with culture and imaging of the joint.** Superficial SSI: clinical. Deep SSI: clinical + culture + imaging.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man is 5 days after an open appendicectomy. His wound is painful and red with a small amount of pus at the lower end. He feels well. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: First-line tests for SSI are a wound swab for culture, FBC and CRP, adding blood cultures only if septic. Imaging is for suspected deep infection.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.
A well patient with a discharging wound: swab the pus and check inflammatory markers.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wound swab, FBC and CRP.

elim: Indicated if he is septic; he is well with normal observations.
For suspected deep or organ/space infection, not a superficial wound with pus.
Not a first-line test for wound infection.
Looks for collections; nothing suggests one here.

steps.x: **E. Wound swab, FBC and CRP.** SSI first-line: swab + FBC + CRP (+ blood cultures if septic).

questions.stem: A 77 year old man is 6 days after an open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. His wound is red with purulent discharge. He is now confused and shivering. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg. The FY1 is about to give intravenous antibiotics.
questions.q: Which investigation should be taken before the first dose of antibiotics?
questions.e: In a septic patient with SSI, blood cultures are taken alongside the wound swab, FBC and CRP, ideally before antibiotics, without delaying them.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.
Septic from an SSI: culture blood before antibiotics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood cultures.

elim: Does not need to precede antibiotics and does not identify the organism.
May be needed later for graft infection but must not delay antibiotics.
Not indicated before treating a septic wound.
Does not identify the organism causing bacteraemia from the wound.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Septic SSI: blood cultures before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman is 9 days after an emergency caesarean section. She has a tender, firm swelling under the Pfannenstiel wound and the overlying skin is red. The wound is not discharging. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. CRP is 160 mg/L despite 3 days of oral antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When abscess or collection is suspected, imaging (ultrasound or CT) is the next step. Ultrasound shows a superficial wound collection quickly.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: tender, firm swelling under the Pfannenstiel wound
steps.x: Not settling on antibiotics with a swelling: look for a collection with imaging.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ultrasound of the wound.

elim: Does not show soft tissue collections.
Will not tell you whether a collection needs draining.
Slow and not the first imaging for a wound collection.
Nothing is discharging, and a swab does not show a collection.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound of the wound.** SSI not settling + swelling = image for a collection (ultrasound or CT).

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is 8 days after an anterior resection with primary anastomosis. He has a swinging fever, rigors and left lower abdominal pain. His wound is clean. His temperature is 38.8°C and pulse rate 112 bpm. Investigations: CRP 260 mg/L (<5), WCC 18.9 x10^9/L (4–11). His CRP trend is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: CRP after surgery
visual.caption: CRP fell after the expected post-operative peak, then rose again: a new infective source.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
questions.e: Suspected organ/space SSI needs imaging; CT abdomen and pelvis finds intra-abdominal collections. A wound swab is useless with a clean wound.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.
Clean wound, swinging fever and rising CRP after bowel surgery: an organ/space collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.

elim: Cannot show a pelvic collection.
Risks the fresh anastomosis and does not show an extraluminal collection.
Do not locate the source.
The wound is clean; the infection is in the operated space.

steps.x: **C. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast.** Suspected deep or organ/space SSI: CT to find the collection.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman is 4 days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Her umbilical port site is red, warm and tender with 2 cm of surrounding erythema. There is no discharge and no swelling. She feels well and is eating. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: How is the diagnosis best made?
questions.e: SSI is a clinical diagnosis; culture and imaging are added only when deep infection is suspected. There is no pus to swab and no swelling to image.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this stage.

clues: red, warm and tender with 2 cm of surrounding erythema
There is no discharge and no swelling
steps.x: A superficial SSI in a well patient is diagnosed at the bedside.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical examination of the wound.

elim: Only if she is septic.
For suspected deep or organ/space infection, not a red port site in a well patient.
Not needed for a superficial infection.
Only needed if a collection is suspected; there is no swelling.

steps.x: **B. Clinical examination of the wound.** Superficial SSI = clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is 5 days after a laparoscopic right hemicolectomy. The extraction wound in her right iliac fossa is red, warm and tender with 4 cm of spreading erythema. There is no pus or fluctuance. She is well. Her temperature is 37.7°C. She has no drug allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Cellulitis around a surgical wound is an indication for antibiotics: first line is flucloxacillin, with clarithromycin if penicillin allergic. There is nothing to drain.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: There is no pus or fluctuance
steps.x: Superficial cellulitis around a wound, no collection, well, no allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral flucloxacillin.

elim: There is no pus or fluctuance to drain.
Too broad for a well patient with superficial cellulitis.
The alternative for penicillin allergy; she has none.
For necrotising or deep infection, not uncomplicated cellulitis.

steps.x: **D. Oral flucloxacillin.** Wound cellulitis: flucloxacillin (clarithromycin if penicillin allergic).

questions.stem: A 44 year old man is 6 days after an open umbilical hernia repair. The wound is red, warm and tender with spreading erythema but no collection. He is well with a temperature of 37.6°C. His notes record a widespread urticarial rash and lip swelling after amoxicillin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Flucloxacillin is first line for wound cellulitis; clarithromycin is the alternative in penicillin allergy. Co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin are penicillins.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: urticarial rash and lip swelling after amoxicillin
steps.x: Penicillin allergy with wound cellulitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clarithromycin.

elim: Contains amoxicillin, which caused his allergic reaction.
A penicillin, so contraindicated in his allergy.
Covers anaerobes only, not Staphylococcus aureus.
A penicillin, and poor against S. aureus.

steps.x: **A. Clarithromycin.** Penicillin allergy + wound cellulitis = clarithromycin.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman is listed for an emergency open appendicectomy for acute appendicitis. She has no allergies and no medical history. The surgical team want to reduce her risk of developing a wound infection after the operation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate measure?
o: Oral antibiotics for 7 days after surgery
Shaving the skin with a razor the night before
Single dose of IV antibiotic at induction of anaesthesia
Topical antibiotic cream on the wound daily
Withholding antibiotics until signs of infection
questions.e: Prophylactic antibiotics at induction reduce SSI in clean-contaminated procedures such as appendicectomy by lowering bacterial load at incision. Long post-op courses add no benefit.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: reduce her risk of developing a wound infection
steps.x: Appendicectomy is clean-contaminated: give prophylactic antibiotics at the time of incision.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Single dose of IV antibiotic at induction of anaesthesia.

elim: Prolonged post-operative courses do not reduce SSI further and increase resistance.
Razor shaving increases SSI; clippers are used if needed.
Not standard practice to prevent SSI.
Misses the benefit of prophylaxis in clean-contaminated surgery.

steps.x: **C. Single dose of IV antibiotic at induction of anaesthesia.** Clean-contaminated surgery: prophylactic IV antibiotic at induction.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is 7 days after an open inguinal hernia repair. The lateral end of his wound is red and bulging with a tense, fluctuant 3 cm swelling. Pus is visible beneath a suture. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. He has already had 3 days of oral flucloxacillin.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Remove sutures over the swelling and drain the pus
questions.e: Pus or a collection must be drained: open the wound, wash out and dress it. Antibiotics alone cannot penetrate an abscess.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: Pus is visible beneath a suture
steps.x: A wound abscess that has not responded to antibiotics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Remove sutures over the swelling and drain the pus.

elim: More antibiotics will not clear a collection of pus.
Does not treat an abscess.
The abscess is obvious on examination; it needs draining, not imaging.
He is not allergic, and antibiotics alone will fail with undrained pus.

steps.x: **D. Remove sutures over the swelling and drain the pus.** Pus = drain it. Antibiotics do not treat an abscess on their own.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman is 4 days after an open sigmoid colectomy. Her wound is red with spreading erythema and pus. She is drowsy. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Change the dressing and review in 24 hours
Sepsis six with IV antibiotics and urgent senior surgical review
Ultrasound of the wound before treatment
questions.e: Assess severity first: she is septic, so she needs the sepsis six, IV antibiotics and escalation to the surgical team, who may take her back to theatre. Waiting for swabs or imaging is wrong.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Septic from an SSI: assess severity, resuscitate and escalate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sepsis six with IV antibiotics and urgent senior surgical review.

elim: Ignores septic shock.
For a well patient with superficial cellulitis, not septic shock.
Imaging must not delay resuscitation and antibiotics.
Delays antibiotics in a septic patient.

steps.x: **C. Sepsis six with IV antibiotics and urgent senior surgical review.** Septic SSI: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, escalate to surgeons.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with peripheral arterial disease is 12 days after a femoral endarterectomy. The groin wound has broken down and contains grey, foul-smelling dead tissue and slough. The graft is not exposed. He is on IV antibiotics and his temperature is 37.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management of the wound?
o: Apply a dry dressing and continue antibiotics alone
Debridement of necrotic tissue with washout and dressings
questions.e: Wound management in SSI includes opening, washout, dressings and debridement of necrotic tissue. Re-suturing is done only once the wound is clean.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: grey, foul-smelling dead tissue and slough
steps.x: Necrotic tissue in an infected wound must be removed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Debridement of necrotic tissue with washout and dressings.

elim: Dead tissue will stay infected unless it is removed.
Closing over infected, necrotic tissue will fail.
Under-treats an open, necrotic wound.
Has no role in wound infection.

steps.x: **B. Debridement of necrotic tissue with washout and dressings.** Necrotic wound tissue = debride, wash out, dress.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is 2 weeks after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. Pus is discharging from the wound, and a sinus tracks down to the prosthesis. She has a temperature of 38.2°C. Investigations: CRP 210 mg/L (<5). Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Return to theatre for washout and debridement
questions.e: Deep or organ/space SSI needs escalation: surgical review and return to theatre for washout and debridement, with IV antibiotics. Oral antibiotics alone fail.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: a sinus tracks down to the prosthesis
steps.x: Deep/organ-space infection of a prosthesis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Return to theatre for washout and debridement.

elim: Oral antibiotics alone cannot clear an infected prosthesis.
Undertreats a deep prosthetic infection.
Ignores a serious deep infection.
A sinus to the prosthesis already shows deep infection; it needs theatre.

steps.x: **D. Return to theatre for washout and debridement.** Deep SSI or infected prosthesis = return to theatre.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man had an infected laparotomy wound opened and packed 10 days ago. He has completed antibiotics. The wound is now clean, with healthy pink granulation tissue and no pus, but it is gaping 8 cm long. His temperature is 36.8°C and CRP is 12 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Repeat wound swab and continue packing indefinitely
questions.e: Wound dehiscence or poor wound closure, once the infection is controlled, needs re-suturing. Further debridement or antibiotics are not needed for a clean wound.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: clean, with healthy pink granulation tissue and no pus
steps.x: Infection treated, but the wound is open.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Re-suture the wound.

elim: There is no dead tissue left to remove.
The infection has resolved.
The wound is clean; it now needs closure.
There is no sign of a collection.

steps.x: **C. Re-suture the wound.** Clean but gaping wound = re-suture.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman is 3 days after a perianal abscess drainage. She has severe perineal pain, far worse than expected. The skin is dusky and there is crepitus extending into the groin. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 130 bpm and BP 84/46 mmHg. IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics have been started.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: CT scan in 24 hours if no improvement
Hyperbaric oxygen as the main treatment
Incision and drainage under local anaesthetic
questions.e: Necrotising soft tissue infection needs emergency surgical debridement alongside antibiotics and resuscitation. Delaying for imaging or antibiotics alone raises mortality.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Necrotising soft tissue infection in a shocked patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Emergency surgical debridement.

elim: Waiting kills; this is a surgical emergency.
At most an adjunct; it does not replace surgery.
Too limited for spreading necrotic tissue.
Wholly inadequate for a necrotising infection.

steps.x: **B. Emergency surgical debridement.** Necrotising infection: antibiotics + emergency debridement in theatre.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man is 6 days after an elective right hemicolectomy. His wound becomes infected, and the swab grows a mixture of Escherichia coli and Bacteroides species. He asks how bowel bacteria got into his wound when he has had no visitors and the ward is clean.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the infection?
o: Airborne spread from another patient after surgery
Bloodstream spread from a urinary catheter
His own gut flora contaminating the wound during surgery
Reactivation of latent infection in the skin
questions.e: SSI results from bacterial contamination of the wound at the time of surgery, usually from the patient's own skin or gut flora. Opening the bowel releases E. coli and Bacteroides.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism or cause: link the clinical clues to the underlying process.

clues: mixture of Escherichia coli and Bacteroides species
steps.x: Bowel organisms after bowel surgery: endogenous flora at the time of operation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: His own gut flora contaminating the wound during surgery.

elim: Airborne spread does not explain bowel organisms in the wound.
Haematogenous seeding of a wound is uncommon and would not give mixed bowel flora.
Food does not seed a surgical wound.
Bacteria do not lie latent in skin this way.

steps.x: **D. His own gut flora contaminating the wound during surgery.** SSI = contamination at operation, mostly endogenous skin or gut flora.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes prednisolone 15 mg daily and methotrexate. Seven days after an open carpal tunnel release her wound is red and discharging, and the skin edges have not healed. Her surgeon notes that her immunosuppression increased her risk.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which her medication increased her risk?
o: Direct toxic damage to the wound by the drugs
Increased skin colonisation with Staphylococcus aureus
Increased tissue perfusion carrying bacteria to the wound
Reduced immune response and impaired wound healing
questions.e: Immunosuppression, like diabetes, obesity and smoking, impairs the local immune response and wound healing, increasing susceptibility to infection.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism or cause: link the clinical clues to the underlying process.

clues: the skin edges have not healed
steps.x: Immunosuppression weakens the local immune response and slows healing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reduced immune response and impaired wound healing.

elim: The drugs work by suppressing immunity and healing, not by direct toxicity.
Colonisation is not the main effect of steroids and methotrexate.
Perfusion is protective, not harmful.
No bleeding is described.

steps.x: **D. Reduced immune response and impaired wound healing.** Risk factors work by impairing perfusion, immunity and healing.

questions.stem: A surgical registrar teaches medical students why surgical site infections are classified as superficial, deep or organ/space. She uses the example of an intra-abdominal abscess after bowel resection, compared with redness around the skin incision.
questions.q: Which statement best explains why organ/space infection is the most dangerous type?
o: It involves the space opened at surgery, with risk of abscess and systemic sepsis
It is always caused by antibiotic-resistant organisms
It is confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissue
It only affects the fascia and muscle layers
questions.e: Organ/space SSI involves the anatomical space entered at operation, so it forms abscesses and causes systemic sepsis; superficial SSI gives local cellulitis and deep SSI involves fascia and muscle.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism or cause: link the clinical clues to the underlying process.
Superficial = skin and fat, deep = fascia and muscle, organ/space = the cavity entered.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It involves the space opened at surgery, with risk of abscess and systemic sepsis.

elim: The organisms are the same skin and gut flora.
That describes superficial SSI.
It often needs drainage or return to theatre.
That describes deep SSI.

steps.x: **A. It involves the space opened at surgery, with risk of abscess and systemic sepsis.** Organ/space SSI is the most dangerous: abscess and sepsis.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man is 2 days after an open repair of a forearm laceration. He has severe pain, rapidly spreading erythema, dusky blistered skin and a temperature of 39.4°C. BP is 88/50 mmHg. Tissue taken at emergency debridement shows Gram-positive cocci in chains growing as a single organism.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Necrotising soft tissue infection can be polymicrobial or monomicrobial; Group A Streptococcus is the classic single organism, seen as Gram-positive cocci in chains.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism or cause: link the clinical clues to the underlying process.

clues: Gram-positive cocci in chains growing as a single organism
steps.x: Monomicrobial necrotising infection with Gram-positive cocci in chains.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus).

elim: Causes antibiotic-associated colitis, not wound necrosis.
A Gram-negative rod.
A Gram-negative rod, not cocci in chains.
Gram-positive clusters, a low-virulence prosthetic organism.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus).** Monomicrobial necrotising infection = Group A Streptococcus.

questions.stem: An infection control nurse reviews 200 wound swabs from patients with surgical site infections after clean orthopaedic and breast operations. The commonest organism grown is Staphylococcus aureus. A student asks why this organism dominates after clean operations.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: It commonly colonises human skin, which the incision passes through
It is spread mainly by contaminated food
It is the only organism killed poorly by prophylactic antibiotics
It lives mainly in the large bowel
questions.e: S. aureus is the commonest cause of SSI because it is prevalent on the skin and contaminates the wound at incision. Bowel organisms matter more after bowel surgery.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism or cause: link the clinical clues to the underlying process.

clues: after clean orthopaedic and breast operations
The commonest organism grown is Staphylococcus aureus
steps.x: Clean operations do not open the bowel, so skin flora dominate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It commonly colonises human skin, which the incision passes through.

elim: Food is not the route into a wound.
Prophylaxis usually covers S. aureus well.
The bowel is home to Gram-negatives and anaerobes, not mainly S. aureus.
That describes necrotising infection, not the reason it is common.

steps.x: **A. It commonly colonises human skin, which the incision passes through.** SSI organism = skin flora, especially S. aureus.

questions.stem: A hospital audit finds that wound infection rates after elective bowel resection fell after the team started giving IV cefuroxime and metronidazole within 60 minutes before the skin incision rather than on return to the ward.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the timing improved results?
o: Antibiotic levels in the tissue are high when contamination risk is greatest
Antibiotics given before incision sterilise the bowel completely
Earlier antibiotics treat established infection faster
Pre-operative antibiotics reduce bleeding at the wound
questions.e: Prophylactic antibiotics reduce the bacterial load at the time of highest contamination risk (incision), so they reduce SSI in clean-contaminated and contaminated surgery. Given later, contamination has already happened.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism or cause: link the clinical clues to the underlying process.

clues: within 60 minutes before the skin incision
rather than on return to the ward
steps.x: Prophylaxis works by being present at the moment of contamination.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antibiotic levels in the tissue are high when contamination risk is greatest.

elim: They reduce, not abolish, bacterial load.
Ileus is unrelated to the antibiotic's effect on SSI.
There is no established infection; this is prevention.
Antibiotics do not affect haemostasis.

steps.x: **A. Antibiotic levels in the tissue are high when contamination risk is greatest.** Prophylaxis must be in the tissue at incision.
